opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, because I use these tools every single day and I've definitely felt both sides of it. On one hand, the productivity gains are real. Things that used to take me an afternoon, like setting up a training pipeline, writing boilerplate for a new experiment, or plotting results, now take minutes. That frees up a lot of mental bandwidth for the parts of research that actually matter, like asking the right questions and designing good experiments.

But I do think there's a real risk of what you might call skill atrophy. If you just accept whatever the model spits out without understanding it, you slowly lose the ability to reason about your own code. And in research especially, that's dangerous, because the bugs that hurt you most are the subtle ones. A wrong normalization, a data leak between train and test, a random seed that isn't actually being set. The code runs, the numbers look plausible, and you're off writing a paper about an artifact.

So my personal rule of thumb is something like: delegate the things you already know how to do, and be much more careful with the things you don't. If I could write it myself and I just don't want to spend the time, great, let the assistant do it, and I can review it quickly because I know what correct looks like. If it's something I genuinely don't understand yet, I try to use the model more as a tutor than as a ghostwriter. I'll ask it to explain, I'll write parts myself, and I'll check things against documentation or small toy examples.

I also think verification is the key skill going forward. The bottleneck is shifting from generating code to checking code. So investing in good tests, sanity checks, small reproducible baselines, all of that becomes more valuable, not less. If you have a strong evaluation harness, you can lean on these assistants much more aggressively, because you'll catch it when they go wrong.

And for students and people early in their careers, I'd say: make sure you still do some things the hard way. Implement a transformer from scratch at least once. Debug something painful without help. That builds the intuition you need to actually supervise these tools well. In a sense we're all becoming managers of AI agents, and a good manager needs to understand the work deeply enough to know when something smells off.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes familiar tasks that can be delegated and reviewed quickly from unfamiliar tasks needing more care, but it does not say automatically accepting generated code is appropriate; it warns against accepting code without understanding it.

r003.rationale: The response discusses adapting to AI’s role in coding, but not continually changing assistant capabilities or the need to continually adapt workflows to those changes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think about this a lot, partly because I use these tools every day and I've watched my own habits shift. The honest answer is that it's a skill question, and the skill is knowing when to lean in and when to pull back.

My rough heuristic is: delegate the things you already understand, and be careful about delegating the things you don't. If I'm writing a data loader or boilerplate for a training loop, I've done that a hundred times, I know what correct looks like, and the assistant is just saving me typing. That's a great trade. But if I'm working on something where I don't yet have a mental model, say a new optimizer or some subtle numerical issue, then letting the model write it for me means I never form that model. I get working code and zero understanding. And the next time something breaks, I'm helpless.

The thing I worry about most is the loss of friction. A lot of learning in research happens because you get stuck. You stare at a bug for two hours and at the end of it you really understand how gradient checkpointing interacts with your memory budget, or whatever. If the assistant removes that friction entirely, you've optimized away the part that made you better. So I try to keep some deliberate friction, especially for junior people in the lab. I'll sometimes say, don't use the assistant for this one, write it yourself, then compare.

The other practical thing is verification. These models are confident and often right, which is exactly the combination that makes you stop checking. I try to treat generated code the way I'd treat a pull request from a very fast colleague who sometimes hallucinates APIs. Read it. Run the tests. Ask yourself whether you could explain every line. If you can't, that's a signal, not necessarily to reject it, but to slow down.

And zooming out, I actually think this is going to bifurcate people. Some will use these tools to compound their understanding, because they ask better questions and read the output critically. Others will use them to avoid understanding, and they'll plateau. The tool is the same. The difference is whether you're using it as a collaborator or as a crutch.

r002.rationale: It says delegation is suitable for familiar boilerplate, but unfamiliar or subtle work needs human understanding and careful verification.

r003.rationale: It discusses adapting one’s habits and preserving understanding, but not changing assistant capabilities that require continual workflow adaptation.

r004.rationale: It does not recommend extensive hands-on interaction as the best way to adapt to changing capabilities.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to keep yourself in the loop intellectually. It’s very easy to get into a rhythm where you ask for some code, run it, get an error, and feed that error back. You can make progress that way, but you can also lose your understanding of what’s actually happening.

For me, a useful test is: can you explain why the solution works, and could you diagnose it if it failed? You don’t need to remember every API, but you should understand the assumptions and have some way of checking the result beyond asking the same assistant whether it’s correct.

And I’d distinguish between trying to finish a task and trying to learn. If you’re learning, struggling with the problem is part of the point. Maybe ask for a hint, or try your own solution before looking at the generated one. If you’re automating something you already understand, you can delegate much more. The important thing is to make that choice deliberately.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to be quite deliberate about what you’re delegating. If the assistant writes some code and you can’t explain what it does or how you would check it, that’s a good moment to slow down. Getting something that runs is different from understanding whether it solves the problem.

For me, a useful habit is to form your own view first: what should the inputs and outputs be, what are the constraints, and where might it fail? Then use the assistant to help implement it or challenge your approach. You still need to inspect the result and test the assumptions.

And it depends on your goal. If you’re trying to learn, struggling with the problem is part of the value, so you probably want hints rather than a complete solution. If you’re building something, you can delegate more, provided you retain the ability to judge what comes back.
